reader.title: Attempted mobbing of Waldo Lewis
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Four men took an accused man from his house at night to a thicket, threatened to hang and shoot him, and fired on him, and a later dispatch called it an attempt to 'mob' him (A1, A4).
Lewis escaped into Morris' house and is not reported killed or wounded, though four men without legal authority threatened to hang him over an alleged theft (A1, A4).
Both reports are specials from Greenville to the Dallas Herald, and the weekly items are reprints of the daily ones (A1, A4; A2, A3, A5).

summary.text: The attempted mobbing of Waldo Lewis took place on the night of October 19, 1881, when four men took Lewis, a young man accused of burglary, from his house near Greenville and threatened to hang and shoot him unless he told where stolen money was hidden.
Lewis escaped into a neighbor's house under gunfire and is not reported hurt, and two of the men were later jailed.
A few days earlier Lewis had been arrested on a charge of burglary and theft of money from a Mr. Merrick.
When his case came before the examining court the trial was postponed, and he was released on bond.
The coverage does not give the race of Lewis or of the men who seized him.
On the night of October 19, Charley Merrick, B. F. Collier, Mike Lackey and a fourth man named only as "Blank" went to Lewis' house, one of them claiming to be an officer.
They carried him six miles to Tidewell thicket and threatened to hang and shoot him if he did not say where the money was.
Lewis told them that part of the money was buried near Sulphur Springs and part in the yard of a Mr. Morris, who lived six miles from Greenville.
When the party reached Morris' house, Lewis ran inside crying murder, and the men fired on him.
Morris demanded their authority for arresting Lewis and, when they showed none, ordered them away.
According to the Greenville correspondent, Lewis' story about the money was "a ruse in order to save his life."
The next morning a party was in Greenville looking for the four men, who had not been found.
By November 3 Collier and Lackey had been arrested and lodged in the county jail.
No report of an arrest of Merrick or "Blank", or of any trial, appears in the coverage.
The episode is known only from the Dallas Herald's Greenville correspondence, where it appeared among notes on cotton receipts, the weather, gaming cases and a wedding.
The daily printed the first dispatch on October 29, and the weekly carried it twice in its November 3 issue.
The arrest notice ran in the daily on November 4 and in the weekly on November 10, where it described Collier and Lackey as "two of the party who attempted to mob Waldo Lewis."
The correspondent offered no comment on the men beyond naming them, and the dispatches made no mention of race.

accounts.label: Greenville correspondent, Oct. 20
accounts.gist: Four men, one posing as an officer, took Lewis out at night, threatened to hang and shoot him to learn where the money was, and fired on him at Morris' house; Lewis' answer was a ruse to save his life.

accounts.label: Greenville correspondent, Nov. 3
accounts.gist: Collier and Lackey, 'two of the party who attempted to mob Waldo Lewis,' were arrested and jailed.

framing.detail: Reported without comment in the 'Greenville' local column; the correspondent treated Lewis' story about the money as a 'ruse' to save his life and later called the act an attempt 'to mob' him.

conflicts.note: The Oct. 20 dispatch was written the next morning and is the better evidence for the date; 'last week' in the Nov. 3 item is loose.
